drip.author: tundrabloom
drip.title: Frost came through two nights ago. The squash leaves are gone, the squash are not.
drip.body:
The warning came at supper, so the harvest happened by headlamp in a toque. By dawn the whole patch was sugared white. The zucchini and squash leaves have collapsed into that dark, wet, boiled-lettuce look, the beans are finished, and the tomatoes I tucked under old bedsheets came through with only a few scorched tips.

Every winter squash is in off the vine and curing somewhere warm. The full-size green tomatoes are in a box in the basement to ripen slowly. The kale is still out there looking smug, because frost only makes it sweeter, and the spinach and radishes I sowed back in the heat are up and don't care about any of this.

Zone 3 gets its goodbye early. It still counts as a whole season if you were there for all of it.

comments.author: solsticegrower
comments.body: We missed it by a degree up here, so every bed is under a sheet and the yard looks like a crime scene with good intentions. Pulled the carrots I need for the week and left the rest in the ground. After a frost or two they taste like they've been dipped in sugar, and they keep better in the soil than in my crisper until the ground starts to freeze.

comments.author: seed_vault
comments.body: If any of those squash are meant for saving seed, let them sit a few extra weeks after curing before you cut them open. The seeds keep maturing inside the fruit. And carry them by the body, never by the stem. A snapped stem is where the rot gets in.

replies.author: tundrabloom
replies.body: Carried two butternuts in by the stem during the headlamp scramble, like a pair of handbags. Noted, with shame.

comments.author: compost_mentis
comments.body: the vines aren't dead, they've just changed departments. soil is a long-term position with excellent benefits

comments.author: brine_shrimp
comments.body: Headlamp harvest in a toque is peak northern gardening. Ours was a light one that only took the basil, which I had been meaning to turn into pesto for two full weeks. The basil ran out of patience before I did.

drip.author: moth_to_a_lamp
drip.title: The houseplant return trip is done. 30 went out, 29 came back, and one slug tried to immigrate.
drip.body:
Back in the summer I asked for everyone's re-entry protocol, and then I followed all of it like a nervous exam student. Hosed down every leaf underside on the balcony, waited three days, and lifted every single pot to look underneath. Found a slug glued under the rim of the big pothos and evicted it with dignity. The whole returning jungle is now in quarantine in the bedroom for three weeks.

The one that didn't come back is the basil, which was always an annual and has gone to the green bin. Everyone else is indoors and deeply unimpressed by the light. The cat is inspecting each returnee like a border officer and has already confiscated one boston fern frond.

No spider mites so far. I check daily with a flashlight and a level of suspicion I normally reserve for my landlord.

comments.author: seed_vault
comments.body: The slug under the rim is exactly why I lift every pot. Twenty-nine clean crossings and one deportation is a very good result.

comments.author: solsticegrower
comments.body: One thing to expect over the next couple of weeks: some yellowing and a few dropped leaves while they adjust to indoor light. It's normal. The trap is watering more to fix it. They're growing slower now, so they want less water, not more. Let the top of the soil dry out and give them time to sulk.

replies.author: moth_to_a_lamp
replies.body: the spider plant yellowed three leaves overnight, clearly to make a point. I am holding the watering can back with both hands

comments.author: compost_mentis
comments.body: rest in peace to the basil. annuals don't fail, they just finish their contract. the green bin is a promotion to soil management

comments.author: tundrabloom
comments.body: Bringing the outside back in is the gentlest chore of autumn. For three weeks your bedroom is a greenhouse with a bed in it, and honestly that sounds lovely.

drip.author: seed_vault
drip.title: Cracking the garlic for planting this week. The biggest cloves go back in the ground.
drip.body:
Every autumn I break apart the best bulbs from the summer harvest, the ones that hung on the drying rack with a string tied around the stems so nobody cooked them by mistake. I only crack them a day or two before planting so the cloves don't dry out.

My method, unchanged in ten years: pointy end up, about 5 cm deep, a hand width apart. Water them in once. Wait until the ground has properly cooled, then cover the bed with straw. The cloves put roots down before freeze-up and then sit there all winter doing nothing you can see, which is the part I like best.

One thing I'd skip is grocery store garlic. It's often grown somewhere with a very different winter, and it can bring disease into your soil that stays for years. Buy from a local grower once, then save your own from then on.

comments.author: solsticegrower
comments.body: Mine goes in this week too. The rule I use up here is a few weeks before the ground freezes hard, which means now, before I find a reason not to. Doubling the bed this year because I ran out of garlic in March and it was a dark month.

comments.author: brine_shrimp
comments.body: Small cloves go to the kitchen, big ones go in the ground, and for once my family fully supports a garlic decision of mine, because nothing about it involves a jar.

comments.author: compost_mentis
comments.body: garlic under straw all winter is the most relatable plant. tucked in, doing nothing visible, technically still working

replies.author: seed_vault
replies.body: Straw, not hay. Hay is full of seed heads and you'll spend June weeding your mulch.

comments.author: tundrabloom
comments.body: Planting something in the fall that you won't see until May is the most hopeful act a northern gardener gets. Mine went in last week under a thick layer of leaves and straw. Zone 3 garlic needs the extra duvet.

late_comments.author: brine_shrimp
late_comments.body: Found this again while pulling out the zucchini this week. Started the milk spray early this year as prevention, before a single spot showed, and the mildew held off until the very end of August instead of turning up in midsummer. Not a cure, but six extra weeks of clean leaves is a trade I'll take. The cafeteria smell also returned, as promised.
